newsitem.title: USA: King County, Wash., considers stadium bond package.
newsitem.headline: King County, Wash., considers stadium bond package.

text.p: King County, Wash., Executive Ron Sims has sent a comprehensive bond package to the county council for consideration to build a new baseball stadium for the Seattle Mariners, his office said on Tuesday.
The package calls for sale and issuance of $336 million in bonds to fund construction of a new Mariners' stadium and adjoining garage, his office said.
A county council committee will consider the package on March 17. Final council action on the package is expected March 25, council spokesman Stephen Kipp said.

"This is another step in the long process towards completing the financing and construction of a first-class, open air stadium for baseball," Sims said in a statement. "I'm forwarding this to the council so they can act quickly and protect taxpayers from the risk of higher interest rates driving up the cost of borrowing for this project."
Last month, King County Superior Court Judge Kathleen Learned upheld the county's plan to issue the bonds to fund the new retractable-roof stadium for the Mariners.
But pending a state Supreme Court review of the decision, Sims said the bond funds would be placed in an escrow account.
"The county's finance team believes it is prudent and important to proceed with the issuance of the bond in order to mitigate certain risks," Sims said.
The King County executive warned that a sharp rise in bond interest rates could cost taxpayers millions more in financing costs over the term of the bonds.
The county's finance team has also expressed concerns about possible Congressional legislation that could restrict the county's ability to issue tax-exempt bonds, Sims said.
The bond sale will be broken into four parts, with three series sold at a fixed interest rate, he said.
The fourth series will be at a variable rate, which may later be converted to a fixed rate bond.

Sims said no additional funds for construction of the ballpark would be released prior to the Supreme Court ruling. If the Supreme Court rules in King County's favor, the escrow funds would be released so construction could begin, he said.

If the bond package is approved by the county counsel on March 25, the county would immediately come to market with the bonds. "The bonds would be sold on the same day," said Frank Abe, a spokesman for the county executive.
